opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is something a lot of researchers underrate. There's this attitude of "the work should speak for itself," but in practice most people will never read your paper. They'll see a tweet, maybe skim the thread, and that's the impression they walk away with. So if you care about your research having impact, communicating it well is part of the job.

My main advice is to figure out the one thing you want people to take away, and lead with that. The first tweet is doing about 90% of the work. A lot of people open with something like "Excited to share our new paper on X!" and a link, and that tells me basically nothing. I want the first tweet to state the core claim, ideally in plain language, ideally with a striking figure. Something like "We found that models represent Y in this surprisingly simple way, and you can use it to do Z." If someone reads only that tweet, they should still come away with the key insight.

Then, visuals matter enormously. A good figure is worth a lot of text, and people scrolling a feed respond to images. So it's worth spending real time making one clean, self-explanatory figure that captures the main result, rather than just screenshotting figure 3 from the paper with tiny axis labels.

For the rest of the thread, I think of it as concentric layers of detail. Each tweet should add something, and someone should be able to stop at any point and still have gotten value. Put the most important caveats and results early, and the methodological detail later for the people who really care.

I'd also stress being honest about limitations. There's real temptation to hype things up, and in a field like interpretability, overclaiming does real damage. People will update on your tweets more than on your carefully hedged discussion section. So I try to flag what we're not confident about, what didn't work, and what the result doesn't show. Ironically, I think that often makes people trust you more.

Some smaller things: tag relevant people and coauthors, make sure the link to the paper is easy to find, and consider posting a short summary or a blog post alongside it, because a thread can only hold so much nuance. Also, don't be shy about promoting your work. A lot of junior researchers feel awkward about it, but if you think the work is useful, helping the people who'd benefit from it actually find it is a service, not self-aggrandizement.

And finally, write it for a smart person outside your subfield. If your thread only makes sense to the ten people who already work on exactly your problem, you've missed most of the audience who could find it interesting or useful.

r001.rationale: The response discusses readers skimming tweets and threads but does not identify clicking to expand a long tweet as a readership barrier.

r002.rationale: It recommends making one clean, self-explanatory figure that captures the main result, so readers can understand it with little surrounding text.

r003.rationale: It recommends a clear figure and cautions against screenshotting figure 3, but does not recommend that the figure typically be the paper’s first figure.

r004.rationale: It recommends writing for smart readers outside the subfield, but does not say that feed readers may not know the author is an ML researcher.

fable-5.1.text:
Neel: Yeah, so I think this is something that a lot of researchers get wrong, and it's kind of a shame, because a good tweet thread is honestly one of the highest-leverage things you can do for a piece of work. Like, I've seen papers that were genuinely good get basically no attention because the authors just posted a link with the title, and I've seen fairly modest results get a lot of attention because someone put real effort into explaining why anyone should care.

The main mental shift is that a tweet thread is not an abstract. People write them like abstracts — "We propose a novel method for X, and show that Y" — and that's the wrong genre. Nobody scrolling Twitter wants to read an abstract. The question you're answering is: why should a busy person who's never heard of you stop scrolling? So the first tweet has to do almost all the work. It needs to be the single most interesting, surprising, or useful thing about the paper, stated in plain language, ideally with a picture. If I can't say what's cool about the work in one tweet, that's often a sign I haven't actually figured out what's cool about the work, which is a problem that goes deeper than communication.

The second thing is that you should write for the person you'd be excited to have read it, not for the reviewers. Reviewers care about novelty and rigor and comparison to baselines. A reader on Twitter cares about "does this change how I should think about something?" or "is there a trick here I could use?" So lead with the takeaway, not the method. Something like "It turns out language models do X, and this was surprising to us because Y" is way more compelling than "We introduce a framework for studying X."

Then structurally, I think of a thread as a funnel. Tweet one is the hook. The next few tweets give the key result and the key figure, and that should be enough for 90% of people — they get the gist, they maybe retweet it, they move on. After that you can go into more detail, caveats, how it connects to other work, and then the link to the paper and a thank-you to coauthors at the end. The people who read all the way through are the ones who actually care, so you can afford to be more technical as you go. But don't front-load the technical stuff, because then you lose everyone.

A few concrete things I'd say. Use pictures, a lot. A figure per tweet, roughly, if you can manage it. A thread that's just walls of text does much worse. Make your figures legible at small sizes — big fonts, few lines, one point per figure. Papers have figures that are designed to be read at a desk; those usually need redoing for Twitter.

Be honest about limitations, but don't bury the lede in them. There's a certain kind of researcher who's so scared of overclaiming that their thread is like "We find weak evidence that, in some limited settings, X may possibly be the case." And I get the instinct — I really don't want people to overclaim, and overclaiming is a real problem in this field. But you can state the result confidently and then be clear about the caveats separately. "We found X. Caveats: this was only on small models, and we're not sure it generalizes" is both honest and readable.

And I think it's worth taking seriously that this is a skill you can practice. My first threads were not good. I'd encourage people to go look at threads that did well from researchers they respect and try to reverse-engineer why. Usually it's some combination of a clear hook, a good figure, and the author actually telling you why they personally found it interesting, which is something the paper format kind of trains out of you.

The final thing I'd say is: if you don't do this, basically no one will do it for you. The default outcome for a paper is that it gets read by a handful of people in your subfield. If you think your work matters — and presumably you do, or you wouldn't have spent months on it — then spending an afternoon making sure people actually hear about it is a very good trade.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention readers needing to click to expand a long tweet or identify that as a readership barrier.

r002.rationale: It recommends using legible figures with one point per figure, but does not say the figure should be understandable with little surrounding context.

r003.rationale: The response does not recommend that the tweet’s figure also be the paper’s first figure.

r004.rationale: The response does not mention that feed readers may not know the author is an ML researcher.

astra-6.text:
I think the most important thing is to give people a reason to care before you get into the details. It’s very easy, when you’ve spent months working on something, to start with the technical problem you were trying to solve. But most people scrolling past don’t have that context. What did you learn, and why is it interesting?

I’d try to make the first tweet stand on its own. Give the actual takeaway, rather than just “We have a new paper!” And then use the thread to explain what you did, show a concrete example, and say what the evidence does and doesn’t establish. If you have a figure that makes the result intuitive, that can be really useful—but you need to explain how to read it.

There’s a balance here: you want to make the work sound interesting, but you don’t want to make a stronger claim than you can defend. I think specificity helps a lot. “We found this particular behaviour in this particular model” can be compelling without implying that you’ve solved the whole problem.

And I’d put effort into making the thread useful even to someone who never clicks through to the paper. Giving them an understanding of the result is already a success.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention clicking to expand long tweets as a readership barrier.

r002.rationale: It recommends using an intuitive figure and explaining how to read it, but does not say the figure should be understandable with little surrounding context.

r003.rationale: It does not recommend using the paper’s first figure in the tweet.

r004.rationale: It says readers may lack context about the research, but does not mention that they may not know the author is an ML researcher.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to give people a reason to care before you ask them to understand the details. It’s very easy, when you’ve spent months working on something, to start with all the context that feels important to you. But someone scrolling past your tweet doesn’t have that context. So start with: what did you find, and why is it interesting?

Then I’d try to give them one concrete example. If you’ve discovered something about how a model works, show a case where understanding that mechanism lets you predict or change its behaviour. That gives people something to hold on to as you explain the more abstract idea.

A thread should also be useful even if someone never clicks through to the paper. Tell them the main result, give some intuition for the evidence, and be clear about the limitations. You can be excited about a result without implying that it establishes more than it does.

And get someone who hasn’t worked on the project to read the draft. Ask them what they think you’re claiming. The gap between what you meant and what they understood is incredibly useful feedback.

r001.rationale: It discusses giving readers a reason to care and making a thread useful without opening the paper, but does not identify expanding a long tweet as a readership barrier.

r002.rationale: It recommends giving one concrete example, but does not recommend communicating research through a figure that is understandable with little surrounding context.

r003.rationale: It makes no recommendation about a tweet figure also serving as the paper’s first figure.

r004.rationale: It notes that readers may lack context, but does not say they may not know the author is an ML researcher.
